statement: Puzzle was the second-largest mobile game genre by IAP revenue in 2025 at $14.4bn, behind Strategy at $20.2bn.
reason: Two separate problems, one of sourcing and one of framing. SOURCING: the $14.4bn and $20.2bn figures appear nowhere in Sensor Tower's own public output. I fetched Sensor Tower's State of Gaming 2026 blog page (https://sensortower.com/blog/state-of-gaming-2026) and its State of Mobile 2026 page (https://sensortower.com/blog/state-of-mobile-2026); both discuss 2025 genre performance qualitatively ("Strategy drove the biggest 2025 revenue gains"; Puzzle showed "strong gains, especially in Europe, with Royal Match reaching the top spot") but publish no genre-level dollar figures. The full report is paywalled. Independent coverage I fetched (Game World Observer, 21 Jan 2026, citing Sensor Tower) corroborates the market total of $81.75bn IAP in 2025 and segment figures for mid-core ($44.68bn) and hybrid-casual ($4.2bn), but carries no Puzzle or Strategy genre figure. PocketGamer.biz returned no coverage of the report at all. So the only trace of these two numbers is the GameDev Reports summary already named in the claim — a secondary source, which the brief instructed me not to rely on. FRAMING: the substack's verbatim sentence is "On mobile in 2025, the strongest growth came from strategy ($20.2 billion) and puzzle ($14.4 billion)." That identifies the two fastest-GROWING genres, with revenue levels in parentheses — it does not rank genres by size, and it does not say Puzzle is second-largest. The same article states "RPG remains one of the largest segments on both mobile and Steam," which directly undercuts the ranking. Sensor Tower's own 2024 subgenre share data (reported by mobilegamer.biz) reinforces the doubt: 4X Strategy just under 10% of total spend, Match-Swap Puzzle 8.67%, Squad RPG 6.14%, MMORPG 5.59%, Casino Slots 5.37%. Rolled up to broad-genre level, RPG (squad + MMO + other RPG subgenres) plausibly sits in the same band as Puzzle, so "second-largest" cannot be asserted. Confidence is LOW on both the figure and the ranking. The dollar values are not demonstrably wrong — they are most likely genre revenue totals from the gated report — so I did not mark this "wrong," but they carry no primary-source backing and the "second-largest genre" claim is an unsupported extrapolation. For an investor deck: cite the $81.75bn market total (well corroborated) and describe Strategy and Puzzle as 2025's fastest-growing mobile genres per Sensor Tower, rather than asserting a genre revenue ranking. If the $14.4bn figure is essential, buy or request the Sensor Tower State of Gaming 2026 report and cite it directly, marking it an analyst estimate.

statement: In H1 2026 puzzle mobile IAP revenue was $8.07bn (up roughly 20% YoY), contributing ~$1.3bn of absolute gain — about 70% of all mobile game revenue growth — while the total mobile IAP market shrank 2.0% to $40bn.
reason: Split result. The MARKET half of the claim is confirmed from the primary source: Sensor Tower's own H1 2026 Gaming Digital Market Index page states "Global Mobile Gaming IAP Revenue hit $40B" with "a 2% decline PoP between H1 '25 and H1 '26," independently corroborated by mobilegamer.biz citing the same report ("Global mobile gaming IAP revenue totalled $40bn in H1 2026, down 2% year on year"). The PUZZLE half could not be independently verified. The $8.07bn figure, the ~20% YoY growth, the ~$1.3bn absolute gain and the ~70% share appear ONLY in the GameDev Reports article named as the source, which I was instructed not to trust; the genre-level breakdown sits inside Sensor Tower's gated 40+ page report, and every Q1 2026 gaming index URL I tried returned 404, so I could not sum the two quarters. Best partial corroboration from a Sensor Tower primary (ungated) page: the Q2 2026 Digital Market Index blog says Puzzle "surged 17% YoY to surpass $4 billion in IAP revenue" in Q2 and was "the only major mobile game genre to achieve positive YoY download growth (+1% YoY)," while overall gaming revenue fell 4.5% YoY. That makes an $8.07bn H1 total arithmetically plausible (implying ~$4.0bn in Q1) and internally coherent ($8.07bn at +20% implies an H1'25 base of ~$6.73bn and a gain of ~$1.34bn, matching the quoted ~$1.3bn) — but plausible is not verified, and Sensor Tower's own published growth rate is 17% for Q2, not "almost 20%." SEPARATE FRAMING WARNING for investor use: because the total market CONTRACTED 2.0%, there was no net market growth, so "about 70% of all mobile game revenue growth" is not a share of net growth. It can only mean puzzle's share of GROSS absolute gains among the genres that grew. Stated unqualified in a deck, that number reads as though the market grew and puzzle captured 70% of it, which the same dataset contradicts. Treat all figures as Sensor Tower estimates (third-party app-store revenue modelling, net of platform fees conventions undisclosed), not audited financials.

statement: Consumer apps are the lowest-raising sector at seed in the 2026 Carta-derived data, with median seed rounds of roughly $1.5M–$2.5M against a national all-sector median of $3.2M at a record $24M post-money valuation.
reason: Contradicted on attribution, timing and substance. (1) The cited report does not exist: Carta's report index (carta.com/data/reports/) lists State of Private Markets, State of Pre-Seed, State of Startup Compensation, VC Fund Performance, Ownership Trends in PE and SPV Spotlight — there is no "State of Pre-Seed and Seed" report. Carta's Q1 2026 releases are "State of Pre-Seed: Q1 2026" and "State of Private Markets: Q1 2026". (2) I read the full text of carta.com/data/state-of-pre-seed-q1-2026/: it covers only unpriced pre-seed SAFEs and convertible notes (~3,000 US startups, $2.3B raised, notes a record-low 7% of rounds, AI at 50% of pre-seed dollars) and contains no seed round-size median, no $3.2M, no $24M and no sector medians. (3) The $24M figure is real but misdated: Carta's own article "Record-setting early-stage valuations" (Kevin Dowd, published 5 March 2026) states "At the seed stage, the median post-money valuation on primary rounds rose to a new all-time high of $24 million in Q4. A year earlier, that figure was $18 million" — that is Q4 2025, and the article adds "These figures span all sectors of the startup economy," i.e. no sector split. (4) Carta's State of Private Markets: Q1 2026 executive summary says "While early-stage primary valuations softened, Series B and Series C primary pre-money valuations are up 17.2% and 12.5%, respectively, since Q1 2025" — contradicting a Q1 2026 "record $24M" framing. (5) Carta's published sector analysis is AI vs applied-AI vs foundational-model by stage, AI concentration by industry, and medians by metro — not seed round size by consumer/fintech/defense/SaaS; its one published seed sector figure is SaaS pre-money valuation by metro (Bay Area $33.3M, NYC $24.5M, rest of US $12.7M, Q1 2026). (6) The other cited sources do not support it either: the Crunchbase News seed-sector piece of 31 July 2026 (news.crunchbase.com/seed/startup-funding-trends-2026-proptech-robotics-cancer-space-tech/) explicitly reports no medians by sector, and the NVCA Q2 2026 Venture Monitor page publishes no seed median deal size. (7) The publisher contradicts itself: Value Add VC's own other page says Carta's Q1 2026 median seed round was $4.1M, "up from $3.2M the prior quarter" — making $3.2M a Q4 2025 number, not a Q1 2026 national median. Caveat: Carta's Round Benchmarking Tool does expose median deal size by stage/sector/region, but its values load client-side and I could not retrieve them, so I could not confirm any specific national or consumer-sector median seed round size from a primary source. Sources actually fetched: https://carta.com/data/record-setting-valuations/ ; https://carta.com/data/state-of-pre-seed-q1-2026/ ; https://carta.com/data/state-of-private-markets-q1-2026/ ; https://carta.com/data/reports/ ; https://carta.com/data/seed-valuations-saas-sf-nyc/ ; https://carta.com/data/state-of-private-markets-q4-2025/ ; https://carta.com/data/explore/round-benchmarking/ ; https://news.crunchbase.com/seed/startup-funding-trends-2026-proptech-robotics-cancer-space-tech/ ; https://nvca.org/pitchbook-nvca-venture-monitor/

statement: Trivia Crack is reported to have more than 600 million downloads worldwide and more than 150 million active users annually, available in 180+ countries and ranking #1 in trivia games in 125 of them.
reason: The cited source does not actually support the claim, and the figure's provenance is a promotional edit. (1) The sentence appears verbatim on English Wikipedia but carries NO inline citation, and the article displays a "may contain original research" maintenance banner. (2) I binary-searched all 341 revisions of the article via the MediaWiki API: "600 million downloads" was introduced on 2021-04-01 by anonymous IP 181.46.138.70 (rev 1015450905). That IP geolocates via ipinfo.io to Quilmes, Buenos Aires, Argentina (AS27747 Telecentro S.A.) — etermax's home city. The diff (compare 1009658666 to 1015450905) shows the editor replaced a referenced, encyclopedic lead with unsourced press-kit boilerplate: "one of the most successful brands in the etermax Gaming division... Board games, consumer products and experiences... complete the experience." That is marketing copy, not a sourced fact. (3) The two language versions contradict each other: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preguntados carries the same boilerplate but states "más de 800 millones de descargas," and explicitly frames it as the sum across multiple franchise games, whereas the English version dropped that framing and attributed the total to "Trivia Crack." The only reference near the Spanish sentence is a Digital Trends "best Apple Watch apps" roundup, which supports the Apple Watch mention, not any download count. (4) The only primary, platform-published number contradicts that scale: Google Play lists the main app (com.etermax.preguntados.lite, developer etermax) at 100M+ downloads with 7.86M reviews; Play's tiers step 100M+ → 500M+ → 1B+, so Android lifetime installs are 100M–500M. The paid Trivia Crack Premium (com.etermax.preguntados.pro) adds only 500K+. (5) I found no support for 150M annual active users anywhere. Etermax is privately held (no SEC filings), and I fetched etermax.com/about and etermax.com/news and parsed the embedded Next.js __NEXT_DATA__ payload — neither publishes any download, user, or country figures. (6) Even taken at face value, the number is a cumulative lifetime franchise install count frozen since April 2021, 5.5 years stale, and cumulative downloads are not active users. Caveat: my WebSearch budget was exhausted at the first call, so I worked via direct fetches (Google Play, Apple iTunes lookup API, MediaWiki API, ipinfo.io, etermax.com); web.archive.org was blocked by egress policy, so I could not check archived etermax press releases that might contain an official figure. That is why I return unverifiable rather than wrong — I can prove the number is unsourced, PR-originated, and self-contradicted, but not that no etermax press release ever stated it. For an investor deck, cite the 100M+ Google Play figure or drop the metric.

statement: Sporcle Events claims 20,000 people each week rely on it for live trivia across the US, but its own live activity widget on 13 September 2026 reported only 75 teams competing and 6 local hosts the previous night.
reason: Verdict is "wrong" because the claim's central contention — that Sporcle's own live widget undercuts its 20,000/week marketing figure — is contradicted by the primary source. Findings: (1) The 20,000 figure is CONFIRMED verbatim at https://www.sporcle.com/events/ : "Today, 20,000 people each week across the nation rely on Sporcle to connect them to their friends." (2) NO live activity widget exists. I fetched https://www.sporcle.com/events/ three separate times with different extraction prompts; every read returned the same complete inventory of on-page numbers (43 founding players in 2009, 45-minute game, 20,000/week, est. 2007, and a footer lifetime counter of 6,819,593,090 quizzes played) and each explicitly reported no live/real-time ticker, dashboard or counter for teams or hosts. I also checked /events/locations/ and /events/the-globe/ — neither carries a live teams/hosts widget. (3) The "6 local hosts" figure is flatly contradicted by Sporcle's own https://www.sporcle.com/events/pub-owner-info/ , which states "500+ Local quiz hosts ready to entertain" and "3,000+ Pub Quizzes run per month" — a national network running ~750 quizzes a week cannot have 6 hosts. (4) Internal consistency supports the 20,000 claim rather than undermining it: 3,000+ quizzes/month is ~750/week, so 20,000 players implies ~27 per event, a normal bar-trivia turnout. Important caveat on method: WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted (200/200) before I could run corroborating searches, and direct curl of sporcle.com returns HTTP 403 (Cloudflare), so I could not inspect raw HTML for a JavaScript-rendered widget. However, even granting a hypothetical JS widget, a "75 teams / 6 hosts" readout would have to be a location-filtered local view rather than a national total, which would make the claim's contrast with a nationwide 20,000/week figure an apples-to-oranges comparison. All figures above come from pages I actually fetched. Note that all Sporcle numbers are self-reported company marketing claims, not audited or regulatory filings — Sporcle is privately held, so no SEC filing exists to independently corroborate the 20,000/week figure.

statement: Blended ARPDAU runs roughly $0.15-0.50 for hybrid-casual games against $0.03-0.08 for hypercasual and $0.01-0.05 for ads-only casual.
reason:
CITATION LAUNDERING — the figure is real but its authority is fabricated by the intermediate source.

Chain traced to origin:
1. Playio Blog (https://blog.playio.co/arpdau-benchmarks-mobile-games) presents the three ranges in a table headed "2026 ARPDAU Benchmarks by Genre and Monetization Model," citing "Game Growth Advisor, F2P Monetization Models 2026" as the "primary source." I fetched this and confirmed the figures.
2. Game Growth Advisor exists but is NOT a research firm — it is gamegrowthadvisor.com, the personal consulting blog of one operator, Cyril Guilleminot. The "F2P Monetization Models 2026" is a blog post, not a report.
3. On his own hybrid-casual post (https://gamegrowthadvisor.com/blog/2026-04-16-hybrid-casual-game-design-strategy-2026/) the sentence appears near-verbatim to the claim: "Blended ARPDAU runs roughly $0.15 to $0.50 for hybridcasual against $0.03 to $0.08 for hypercasual." Crucially, his own source-attribution table labels it "GGA canonical reference set, moderate confidence," and on the monetization post he explicitly says these are "the bands I am willing to plan against" rather than industry consensus, noting that many published benchmarks lack primary sources. He also warns the gap "spans 1.9x to 16.7x, so no single multiplier describes the gap honestly."
4. Playio stripped that caveat and re-labelled operator judgment as a "benchmark" with a "primary source." The claim inherits Playio's framing.

Primary sources checked — none state these ranges:
- Tenjin, "Ad Monetization in Mobile Games — Benchmark Report 2026" (https://tenjin.com/blog/ad-mon-gaming-2026/): 146bn ad impressions, but reports eCPM and revenue share only. No ARPDAU at all.
- GameAnalytics 2026 Mobile & PC Gaming Benchmarks (https://gameanalytics.com/benchmarks/): gated, no figures public.
- Appodeal live benchmarks tool (https://appodeal.com/benchmarks/): returns "No data available for the selected filters."
- Appodeal 2025 Mobile Casual Benchmarks (10,000+ games, Jun 2024–Jan 2025, US Android; https://gameindustrylibrary.com/documents/mobile-casual-benchmarks-report-2025): reports ARPU, not ARPDAU — hypercasual/simulation $0.79, hybrid-casual subgenres $11.08–$14.83. Different metric (lifetime, not daily); cannot be used to support the claim.
- AppsFlyer State of Gaming (https://www.appsflyer.com/resources/reports/gaming-app-marketing/) and Liftoff 2025 Casual Gaming Apps Report (https://info.liftoff.ai/2025-casual-gaming-apps-report): both gated, no genre ARPDAU public.
- The upstream sources GGA names (TopOn H1 2025, AppsFlyer 2026, Matej Lancaric June 2025) could not be found publishing genre ARPDAU; lancaric.me has no such post.

Two secondary sources contradict the internal ordering:
- Juego Studios (https://www.juegostudio.com/blog/arpdau-benchmarks-by-game-genre), citing AppsFlyer/GameAnalytics/Liftoff/Appodeal 2024–25, puts hyper-casual at $0.01–$0.05 and casual/puzzle at $0.03–$0.10 — the REVERSE of the claim, which puts hypercasual above casual.
- AppSamurai (https://appsamurai.com/glossary/arpdau/) assigns $0.15–$0.50 to MID-CORE games, and casual ad-based to $0.01–$0.05.

So the $0.15–$0.50 band is elsewhere attached to a different genre entirely, and the hypercasual/casual ordering is disputed. The directional claim (hybrid-casual out-earns hypercasual per DAU) is uncontroversial and well supported in principle; the specific numbers are one person's planning assumptions with no measured backing. Marking unverifiable rather than wrong, since no primary source refutes them either — but they must not be presented to investors as a benchmark.

statement: Trivia games show above-average app store listing conversion at 8.2% on iOS and 20.4% on Android, versus 3.2% and 14.3% for casual games generally.
reason:
TRACED THE CITATION CHAIN TO ITS PRIMARY SOURCE. Mistplay (fetched at the claimed URL, published 10 Apr 2026) does print exactly the quoted numbers — 8.2%/3.2% iOS and 20.4%/14.3% Google Play — but it is a tertiary source: it credits Business of Apps, which in turn credits AppTweak as the data originator.

Business of Apps ("App Conversion Rates (2026)", David Curry, updated 26 Jun 2026, https://www.businessofapps.com/data/app-conversion-rates/) has its tables paywalled, but its free "Key Statistics" section states: "Food and drink apps had the highest conversion rate on iOS at 52.8%, while social networking apps had the lowest at 9.8% (Apptweak)" and "Puzzle had the highest conversion rate for games on iOS, on Google Play it was education apps."

I then went to AppTweak itself ("Average App Conversion Rate per Category [2025]", published 18 May 2026, updated 6 Aug 2026). Its body text says plainly: "the lowest average conversion rate [was] in the Games – Trivia category, with an average CVR of 5.2%" against a US App Store all-category average of 8.56%. The per-category figures live in three Infogram embeds; I pulled the underlying chart JSON directly (e.infogram.com/771fba68-f641-4494-bea8-2be0ceb30915 for iOS CVR, b4520472-dc21-4b5e-a027-1905647d7791 for Google Play CVR, 4ce4e029-9cd7-4f1e-9bd8-923c3fe83a89 for iOS install rate). Verbatim values: iOS — Games-Trivia 5.2%, Games-Casual 34.1%, Games-Puzzle 35.7%, Games-Board 35.6%, Games (all) 26.7%. Google Play — Games-Trivia 19.8%, Games-Casual 11.4%, Games-Educational 33.8%, Games (all) 19.9%, Games-Strategy 6.6%. iOS impression-to-install rate — Trivia 2.60%, Casual 1.10%.

THREE INDEPENDENT REASONS THE CLAIM IS CONTRADICTED, NOT MERELY IMPRECISE:
(1) Directionally inverted on iOS. The claim's whole point is that trivia beats casual and beats the average on iOS. AppTweak shows trivia at 5.2% — dead last of ~38 categories, below the 8.56% average — while casual sits at 34.1%, i.e. casual converts 6.5x BETTER than trivia on iOS. The claim has the ranking backwards.
(2) The casual iOS figure is off by an order of magnitude: 3.2% claimed vs 34.1% actual.
(3) Mistplay's iOS table is internally inconsistent with the source it names. It lists Puzzle at 2% and Board at 1.2% (near the bottom), whereas Business of Apps — the source Mistplay explicitly credits — states Puzzle is the HIGHEST-converting iOS game genre, matching AppTweak's 35.7%. Mistplay's Google Play table is closer but still shifted (it gives Music 45% and Educational 40.6% vs AppTweak's 26.8% and 33.8%), suggesting Mistplay used a stale or mismatched vintage of the dataset.

WHAT SURVIVES: only the Android half of the directional claim. Trivia at 19.8% on Google Play genuinely is above the 16.15% all-category average and above casual's 11.4%, and the claimed 20.4% is within rounding distance of 19.8%.

CAVEATS FOR DECK USE: AppTweak's benchmarks are vendor-measured estimates (AppTweak Conversion Rate Benchmarks feature), not audited data, and are US-only for calendar 2025 — they should be attributed to AppTweak by name. Note also the metric definition trap: AppTweak's "conversion rate" is page-views-to-install, while "install rate" is impressions-to-install (trivia 2.6%, casual 1.1% on iOS); the claim does not specify which, and the two differ by more than 10x. The IPM half of the claim (trivia 10.3 vs 8.62 global average) remains unverified: Mistplay attributes it to Adjust's 2025 gaming apps report, but that report is a gated download, adjust.com returned 403/429 to every fetch attempt, and the archived Adjust landing page (web.archive.org snapshot 20250911160422 of adjust.com/blog/gaming-app-insights-2025/) states only headline stats (global installs +4% YoY in 2024, strategy installs +83%) with no IPM figure. Do not put the IPM numbers in an investor deck on this sourcing.

statement: Widely-circulated global fan-base estimates put soccer at 3.5 billion fans, cricket at 2.5 billion, basketball and hockey at 2 billion each, and tennis at 1 billion.
reason: I fetched the cited page and confirmed it states exactly these figures, so the claim is an accurate description of what circulates. But the task was to find the numbers from a primary source, and none exists. Sources I actually fetched: (1) https://www.topendsports.com/world/lists/popular-sport/fans.htm — states all six figures; self-describes them as "estimated global fan bases" that "may vary based on methodology and regional definitions," and notes the 2B hockey figure only works by merging field and ice hockey. (2) https://www.topendsports.com/world/lists/popular-sport/index.htm — the same site's methodology hub admits the world's-most-popular-sport question "possibly has never been definitively determined" and that it found its numbers via "a quick search online," citing no named survey, federation report or research firm. That makes Topend Sports an aggregator of other websites, not a data source. (3) https://www.icc-cricket.com/ and https://www.icc-cricket.com/media-releases — the ICC publishes no global fan figure; its site refers to "cricket's global fan community" with no number. (4) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket — states "cricket's fanbase cross one billion people, with 90% of them in South Asia"; I pulled the raw wikitext (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cricket&action=raw) to trace the citation to ESPNcricinfo, "ICC survey reveals over a billion fans - 90% in subcontinent," 27 June 2018, reporting the ICC's own global market research. (5) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket_in_South_Asia raw wikitext independently cites the Indian Express, 28 June 2018, "Cricket has 1 billion fans, 90% of them in subcontinent," for the same ICC 2018 research. Two independent citation trails to the same ICC study at ~1B directly contradict the 2.5B cricket figure. (6) https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_football&action=raw — FIFA's own cited primary figures are ~250 million active players (FIFA Big Count survey) and 2014 World Cup reach of 3.2 billion viewers with 1 billion for the final; both are FIFA-published, and neither is a 3.5-billion fan base. Reach-of-a-tournament and standing-fan-base are different metrics. (7) https://www.fiba.basketball/en/about-fiba (404) and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball — no global basketball fan or player count published. Constraint to flag: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before I began, and the agent proxy repeatedly reset connections to DuckDuckGo and returned unrelated results from Bing, so I could not run keyword searches; findings rest on direct fetches of federation sites, the source page, and Wikipedia wikitext used only to trace citations back to their primary sources. ESPNcricinfo and Indian Express both returned 403 to direct fetch, so the ICC ~1B figure is confirmed via two independent citation trails rather than the underlying articles themselves — which is why I set unverifiable rather than wrong. Verdict is unverifiable, not confirmed, because no primary source states any of these six numbers; and not wrong, because the claim is hedged as "widely-circulated estimates," which is literally true. The cricket figure is the one actively contradicted by the sport's own governing body.
